question.problem:
Find $\text{E}[{X}^{2}+2Y],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2},\, & 0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonzero only in the rectangular region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1\}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X{Y}^{2}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}({x}^{2}+2y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+2y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+2y)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{4}{3}+2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\frac{4}{3}y+{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
